 Asmongold’s 9-hour GTA VI video drew 2.36m views on launch day, and 14,000 comments 
 Intermission 
 Asmongold, a GTA first-timer, rates GTA VI a nine after nine hours
 Asmongold's 9-hour GTA VI VOD drew 2,358,707 views and 14,000 comments, topped by an 11,000-like protester claim the video never shows. What are brands buying?
 by Luis Rijo 
 Luis Rijo

 Asmongold TV today published "So I Played GTA 6..", a recording that runs to just over nine hours in which the streamer Asmongold, who tells viewers he has never played a Grand Theft Auto game, works through the opening of Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI on an Xbox and ends with a verdict: "I would rate it like a nine." By 20:02 UTC, the video page showed 2,358,707 views, 83,324 likes and 14,000 comments, and placed the upload at No. 28 on YouTube's trending list for video games.
 Grand Theft Auto VI went on sale today. For the advertising trade, the score matters less than the world the recording walks through. Rockstar's fictional state of Leonida has a photo app called Snapmatic that lets one character "ingest everything about a person", a bank that refuses an account and points the customer to a phone app called Buck Me, a ride-hailing app called RideMe and a radio station that jokes about sponsorship. The comment section under the video argued about other things. Its most-liked comment, with about 11,000 likes and 813 replies, says the game stops a car driven at protesters, a scene the recording never shows, and much of the rest repeats, in harsher words, Asmongold's own running joke that the game was written by women.
 In Short
 Asmongold, whose YouTube channel has 4.76 million subscribers, posted a nine-hour first playthrough of Grand Theft Auto VI on the game's release day, rated it "like a nine" and said it would probably win game of the year, while saying it should not because it is not on PC. The video drew more than 2.3 million views within hours and is the kind of long, unscripted creator content that brands buying gaming audiences around a major launch have to judge, in a game that itself parodies social media, fintech apps and ad-funded radio. Under it, a comment section of more than 14,000 comments is led by complaints about limits on violence, "HR women" and the two leads, and none of the 20 comments the page displayed at 20:02 UTC mentions those parodies. The public view count now includes YouTube's estimate of people watching together on a TV and registers from the first frame, so it says little about how much of a nine-hour video anyone actually watched.
 The video and its numbers
 The upload sits on Asmongold TV, the streamer's main YouTube channel. According to its description, "Asmongold plays GTA 6 (Grand Theft Auto VI) for the first time, exploring Vice City and the open world of Leonida in Rockstar Games' long-awaited release." The description credits two channel editors, "CatDany & Daily Dose of Asmongold", and lists the places where the streamer broadcasts and republishes: a Twitch channel under the handle zackrawrr, a Kick channel, an X account, a subreddit, and two "VOD Rerun" channels, one on Twitch and one on Kick.
 Two other lines in the description concern money and rights. One is an affiliate link for a gaming guide add-on unrelated to Grand Theft Auto: "Download the fastest leveling guide on the market which seamlessly integrates into your in-game RestedXP addon and get 10% off with my link." The other is a takedown route: "If you own the copyright of content showed in this video and would like it to be removed:", followed by two X accounts belonging to the editors. The page tags the video with a single game, Grand Theft Auto VI, dated 2026.
 The oldest comments on the page were marked as posted 14 hours before 20:02 UTC, which puts the upload in the early hours of November 19.

 How much those 2,358,707 views say about attention is a separate question. YouTube began including an estimate of people watching together on a TV in public view counts this month , and a view registers when playback starts, across long-form videos, Shorts and live streams. YouTube says Partner Program earnings still run on engaged views rather than on the public number. For a nine-hour recording, the counter therefore records starts, partly modelled, and nothing about how far into the session anyone stayed.
 The captions are YouTube's automatic transcript, and they carry no speaker labels. Game dialogue, the streamer's commentary and viewer messages that he reads aloud run together in the same lines, so the attributions in this article are made from context. Profanity appears in the captions as "[ __ ]", and quotes below keep that placeholder where it falls.
 A first-timer on an Xbox
 Asmongold returns several times to the fact that this is his first Grand Theft Auto. "I've never played a Grand Theft Auto game before in my life," he says an hour and a half in. At 5:47:22 he extends the point to the genre: "I've never played Saints Row." In the closing review he puts the caveat on the record: "But this is my first um this is my first GTA game that I've ever played."
 The platform was a choice of timing rather than preference. Asked by a viewer at 1:59:57 whether he is on a PlayStation, he answers: "No, it's an Xbox." At 5:08:23 he explains why, after reading out a viewer's complaint that the game "runs like ass on Series X": "It's because people said I couldn't do that New Zealand [ __ ] on a PS5. They said I can only do it on a uh on an Xbox." The remark appears to refer to setting a console's region to New Zealand, one of the first places where midnight on a release date arrives, to start playing early. The stream does not show how the game was unlocked.
 The Xbox detail has a commercial echo. On October 28, Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella pointed to GTA VI arriving on Xbox in November , in a quarter when Xbox revenue fell 2% to $5.38bn.
 Performance barely registers in the commentary. When a viewer asks "How does the 30 fps feel?", the answer is "It's nothing. It's really nothing." Later he adds: "Like maybe like the first five minutes I noticed it, but then it's like you just get used to it and then that's just the game." The controller is another matter. "I can't aim with a controller. I really can't," he says at 5:07:19, and near the end he spells out what he would rather have: "I want to play it on a computer at 120 FPS with high-end graphics and aim with a mouse and have it on Steam and that's it, you know?" A viewer's message read aloud claims a PC version will arrive in the first quarter of next year. Nothing on the stream confirms that date.
 What the stream shows of the game
 The recording is a long first look at the game's opening chapters, and the on-screen prompts and dialogue the streamer reads out record a set of systems that will matter to anyone writing about, sponsoring or advertising around the game. According to the transcript, they are:
 Neighbourhood restrictions. Jason Duval, the first of the two leads, lives in a stilt house in the Keys. A prompt at 1:06:44 states: "Vehicles in your neighborhood can't be stolen." It returns at 2:10:30. A second prompt, garbled in the captions, says a weapon cannot be equipped "while you're in your neighborhood."
 Police dispatch. "Crime reported" warnings follow traffic offences. At 2:18:51 a character installs an app on Jason's phone with the line: "Now you'll be able to see when and where the cops are being dispatched."
 Cash, a home stash and a bank. Money is deposited in a hidden stash at the house, with a "Cash deposit" option at 2:56:41. At 5:17 a bank turns Jason down and offers a phone-only account instead, described below.
 Vehicle damage and repair. Cars lose wheels and durability, are totalled, and are repaired and resprayed at garages. One garage owner offers to tow Jason's car and put it "on Brian's account."
 Shopping and appearance. A haircut costs "$60". Outfits can be saved with a "Save current outfit" option. Flowers and a custom necklace spelling the name of Lucia's son, Tomas, are ordered for delivery, the necklace in "a couple of days."
 House repairs and a relationship meter. Once Lucia Caminos, the second lead, is released from the Hamlet Correctional Facility, a run of household tasks opens up: fixing a railing, repairing a leaking roof and repainting walls, with the choice "Pastel peach, stormy blue, or tropical green." At 6:15:40 the streamer reads out the result: "It says house repairs complete and then I got the plus heart." Earlier, at 4:48:01, he asks why he has just lost a heart.
 Side activities. The transcript records pool, a bar fight, dancing, a dating app ("Just checking the field. Swiping my way to success"), workouts ("Finish the workout"), meditation on a dock and games played on a friend's console.
 Ride-hailing. At 5:30:43 a prompt reads: "You can use the RideMe app to order a ride." The fare on screen is $26. "$26. Are you kidding me?" the streamer says, and walks.
 Leonida's ad economy
 Grand Theft Auto has long parodied the businesses that fund American media, and the transcript shows the new game aiming at the ones PPC Land covers every day: social platforms that harvest personal data, fintech apps that serve people banks turn away, gig work, wellness resellers, AI and sponsored audio.

 Data, scrolled
 The sharpest line on personal data comes from Mandy, a tenant whose blocked sink Jason has to clear before she will pay the rent. "It's just so crazy what you can learn from a little scrolling on Snapmatic," she says. "You can just like ingest everything about a person." Everything, she goes on, "like what kind of music they listen to or they used to date or where they work out." Jason answers: "Yeah, I think that is called stalking, Mandy." Her reply: "Nuh-uh. It's not stalking if you've met in person."
 A second social network appears four hours later. Cal, Jason's friend, shows him their landlord Brian's phone. "Dude was all over his ex-wife's life invader," Cal says. "Anyway, he liked a few photos, you know, left a few comments." Brian, by Cal's account, "Came to old Uncle Cal to make it look like it never happened."
 Banks, credit and an app
 The fintech satire is the most developed in the recording. Lucia needs a bank account for her prison work wages, and Jason does not have one. At the bank, an employee tells him his credit is "dog [ __ ]" and says: "The computer won't even let me get you an account, much less one of our mortgage products." The alternative is an app. "The best thing I can do is set you up with some Buckme accounts. It's on your phone. There are transaction limits," the employee says, adding: "build your credit up and I'll be able to get you a real account. Until then, my hands are tied."
 The app opens with "Welcome to Buck Me." An advert follows on the phone, captured mid-sentence by the captions: "Your family's future by opening a Buck family account today. See online for details." Lucia then relays Cal's theory of retail banking: "You know, Cal says that banks use your late fees to fund pleasure cruises for washed up celebrities and war criminals."
 Rent collection gets the same treatment. "You know, it's really annoying that Brian makes everyone pay the rent manually," Mandy says, complaining that it happens "on a sketchy little website that looks like it was made by a fifth grader." Her verdict: "Like, hello. Ever heard of autopay?"
 Work, wellness and AI
 Mandy also announces a promotion. "I'm chief director of product now," she says, and "I manage like a million engineers, but I'm totally work from home." Andy, a friend of Lucia's who works at a restaurant, has a second job: "I give people access to great wellness products without the crazy overhead of retail. It's been super lucrative so far." Neighbours argue about short-term lets. "People rent out their houses," one says. The other calls the house next door "a goddamn revolving door" with "a different set of strangers every weekend."
 AI turns up twice. Cal introduces an independent game made "in a log cabin in Liberty State" with the words "The design, the code, the art. He even did the voiceover." A line the captions do not attribute adds: "He didn't even use AI." Cal dismisses the alternative as "any of that AAA corporate ass juice". Later, on a television show Jason and Lucia watch, a contestant explains away a message: "It was a bot. You think I have time to chat with everybody on my peole?" The captions garble the name of the platform.
 Outside the game, the same subject surfaced in the closing chat. A viewer's message read aloud claimed that Rockstar was "panicking about vibecoded versions of GTA 6 popping up. So they're rushing release." Asmongold's response: "I don't believe that. I think that's ridiculous." He then observed that "a lot of the other delays weren't happening during the uh reverse engineer vibe coding era, right?" The reference is to vibe coding , building software by prompting an AI model. No evidence for the claim appears on the stream.
 Sponsorship on the radio
 The radio stations carry their own jokes about who pays. On Emotion 98.3, the presenter says: "We go through so many tissues here at Emotion 98.3." The next line, "I'm surprised Day isn't sponsoring this station," garbles the name of the sponsor in question. A public information spot on shark safety ends: "For more information, visit leonaggov.org/sharks safety. Paid for by the American Rifle membership." The web address is clearly mangled in the captions.
 Real brands enter the recording through the commentary rather than the game. While assembling a coffee table with Lucia, the streamer calls it building "IKEA", and during the house repairs a line on the stream jokes that the sequence feels "sponsored by Home Depot". Neither company is named in the game dialogue captured in those scenes, and the video description lists no sponsor for the upload.
 Asmongold on the chores and the writing
 The household tasks drew the most commentary from the streamer. "I'm getting domesticated," Asmongold says at 3:47:11, after a run of errands for Lucia's release, a line the captions surround with references to being an "Aaron boy", their rendering of errand boy. Repainting the house more than two hours later, he asks: "What are they doing? The whole house? I don't I get a day off or something?" Shopping for Lucia, he narrates his own role: "Yeah, I'm trying to simp out, guys. I really am."
 He also ran a joke all day about who wrote the game. Nineteen minutes in, when Jason talks about booking a conjugal visit, he says: "No, that's how you know this [ __ ] was written by women. His girlfriend's in jail for 2 years. He's not hooking up with other girls." Six hours in, he stopped to address what he was seeing online. "I have got to play GTA 5 cuz I want to know like cuz there's people crashing out about this. I looked at Twitter," he said, before calling Jason "your traditional like simp like boyfriend" and adding: "It feels like it's kind of a uh you know like a female fantasy, right? But like I don't really think it's been bad." He went on: "I don't want people to get the wrong idea that I like hate it or I don't like I don't like the game or I don't think it's fun."
 Asked at 7:19:51 whether the game was worth getting, he said: "I think that the criticisms about the game kind of having like it being written by women. I think it's true. I do. I think it is true. But there's some funny stuff and parts of it too". In the closing review he called the Jason and Lucia dialogue "written by a chick" and then qualified it: "But I mean like I joke I joke about it a lot, right? Cuz it's funny to make fun of it. But it's not like it was really that bad." The recording contains no information about who wrote the game's script. He also predicted the wider argument: "I'm sure there's going to be people talking about uh you know, it being woke or whatever. Like that always happens."
 After a line that appears to be a viewer's message, "I don't understand the hate. It makes no sense.", he set out the complaints he had seen as he understood them: "they don't like the fact that Jason seems like he takes a backseat role and it seems like he's obedient towards Lucia." He went on: "It seems like also Lucia just makes a series of bad decisions while Jason convinces her not to and plot armor saves her from the consequences of those bad decisions." Asked whether he found Lucia annoying, he answered: "Yeah, I do. But like I think that's part of the point, right?" and added: "Like I think both the characters are stupid, right?"
 He also mentioned reports he had not checked. "I've seen like some of the other stuff about like somebody says you can't shoot protesters and you can't buy hookers and stuff like that. I don't really know how much of that's true," he said, adding that "nowadays I'll like see clips of like streamers saying things and then I'll look at I'll watch the clip and it's like they didn't even say what the clip said they said." The transcript contains no scene with protesters.
 What the comments say
 At 20:02 UTC the page showed a count of 14,000 comments and displayed 20 of them, in YouTube's own order, which was not ranked by likes. Like counts above 1,000 are rounded on the page, so the figures below are approximate. PPC Land does not reproduce two of the 20: one, with about 5,900 likes, jokes about suicide, and the other, with about 2,000, jokes about the killing of children.  Limits on violence
 The most-liked comment on the page is a claim about a game mechanic: that the game slows a car to a stop when the player tries to drive into a group of protesters. Its likes, about 11,000, equal about 13% of the 83,324 likes on the video itself, and its 813 replies outnumber the replies to the other 17 quoted comments combined, which total 658, according to PPC Land's count. The recording does not show such a scene, and Asmongold said on stream that he did not know whether the claim was true. The restrictions the recording does document are narrower: in Jason's neighbourhood, vehicles cannot be stolen and a weapon cannot be equipped.
 The two other comments in the group, "Remember When GTA Was About Doing Whatever You Want?" and @matthewdancz9152's contrast between violence against police and against protesters, match a viewer message Asmongold read aloud near the end: "Feels more limited and restrictive compared to previous GTA. It focuses more heavily on characters." His answer was that he had mostly stuck to the main story, "because I figured like let's go with the main story and just see what that's going to be about."
 "HR" and the writers
 The second-largest group repeats, in harsher terms, the joke Asmongold had made all day. @Deminisis wrote that "HR women determine the acceptable crimes you're allowed to commit". Three hours later, @irenaenriette posted a reworded version of the same sentence, which drew 933 likes; the page does not show whether that account copies other users' comments. @daydos_soundscapes called the game "A women's interpretation of Grand theft Auto". @kebab9111 contrasted the opening of Grand Theft Auto V, "for actual adults living in the real world", with the new one, "for theater kids and HR", and wrote that "Asmon needs to try gta V". Viewers had pressed the same point during the stream, in messages Asmongold read out such as "You'll enjoy GTA 5 for Trevor alone", and he had said he would play it. None of the comments offers evidence about who wrote the game.
 Lucia and Jason
 "Press X to empathize with Lucia's struggles" and "GTA 6: deadbeat mom and her abused husband" restate, as jokes, the complaints Asmongold summarised in his review: that Jason seems "obedient towards Lucia" and that she "makes a series of bad decisions". @EDP91's complaint about being "forced to have to play as a simp" uses the word Asmongold had used for his own role. @savageaminal1715 wrote that "If this game had real writers", the story would include ICE trying to deport Lucia, a storyline the recording does not contain. The newest comment visible, posted 40 minutes before 20:02 UTC, prefers a different character: "The real crime was choosing Lucia over Mandy", the tenant from the Snapmatic scene.
 Chores and time off
 Four comments join the housework to the time people took off to play. "everyone took sick leave just to do chores in GTA VI" and "Imagine taking a day off from being a handyman to play as a handyman" mirror Asmongold's own question during the repainting: "I don't I get a day off or something?" @FercPolo's "13 years to make GTA a 'cozy' game" applies a label usually given to relaxed life-simulation games. The time-off jokes sat alongside YouTube's own recommendations. Beside the video, YouTube suggested a CNN segment whose title says Grand Theft Auto VI "could cost $1B in US" productivity, and a Bloomberg Originals film, "Why the Stakes for GTA VI Are So High", shown with 2 million views.
 Watching instead of playing
 @d_j_c009's "So glad Asmongold is playing this so I don't have to", with about 5,300 likes, describes the arrangement behind the whole format: the streamer plays and the audience watches. Asmongold made a related point about how the game looks from the outside: "It seems too easy. That's probably just cuz you're watching me play, which makes sense, right?" He added: "it's really not that hard." The one comment outside the main themes, @steel6322's Tiger King remark, apparently refers to the tigers in the game's opening missions, where one character asks another: "Hey, you still got those tigers?"
 What the comments leave out
 None of the 20 comments displayed mentions Asmongold's score, the Xbox, the frame rate or a PC version. None mentions Snapmatic, Buck Me, RideMe, the radio stations or any other part of the game's satire of social media, fintech and advertising. The most-liked comments were also the oldest: the five posted 12 to 14 hours before 20:02 UTC hold about 34,100 of the 47,700 likes on the 18 quoted comments, about 71%, while the five posted two hours or less before had fewer than 200 likes each.
 The verdict
 The review comes in the last 20 minutes. "I would rate it like a nine. I think it was good," Asmongold says. Asked which game earns a 10, he names Elden Ring. He is less kind about the writing, using a term the captions render as "fam slop": "I think some of the story stuff is like kind of I think it's like kind of fam slop, right? Like and Jason isn't like that great of a character." When a viewer's message read aloud warned that playing Grand Theft Auto V would make this one look badly written, he answered: "No, I already think the game is badly written. That's why I didn't give it a 10."
 On awards, he separates prediction from preference. "I think it's going to win game of the year, right?" he says. "Yeah, it will." Then: "You know why I don't think it should win game of the year is cuz it's not on a computer."
 He hedges on depth. "I would say that the combat seems kind of simple, but that also could be my fault," he says, noting that he "used the pistol for 95% of the game." He compares the structure to Cyberpunk and, earlier in the stream, to Crimson Desert. "I just don't know if the game is simplistic because of my way of playing the game or the game's simplistic because the game's simplistic."
 He also states a principle that cuts against long games that improve slowly: "I think if something is going to be good, it's going to be good immediately." Asked whether he would recommend it to a friend: "Yeah. Yeah, sure. I'd recommend it." Asked whether it justifies buying a console: "That's up to you," because "you don't know somebody's financial situation."
 The most useful remark for anyone who pays creators to play games comes in the final minutes. "Maybe the fact that I'm playing the game on stream makes me have a better opinion of it because I view the stupid things in the game as content rather than just an annoyance," he says. "If I was playing this privately, like just by myself, I would probably be annoyed by that." The chores that annoyed the comment section were, on his account, good material for a broadcast.
 On format, he draws a line under marathon streams. "I don't like doing marathon streams," he says, and "I almost never go over like 10 hours just because I think that's how you can burn yourself out." He allows an exception: "If there's any game to do it, then I feel like this is the game to do it." He signs off saying he expects to go live again tomorrow "between 11:00 and 12:00".
 Why this matters for marketers
 The video lands in the middle of a launch that platforms and publishers have been planning around for months. On November 12, YouTube said videos about Grand Theft Auto VI had passed 40 billion views before release and set out a launch week built on its own programming: five limited-edition Live gifts, one of them free, a Vice City Shorts effect and a 24-hour stream on its own channel from midnight Eastern time today. Asmongold's upload shows the other way creator attention reaches YouTube on a launch day: a long recording from a streamer whose description sends live viewers to Twitch and Kick.
 Those platforms are moving in different directions. Streams Charts data for the third quarter put Twitch at 4.51 billion hours watched, up 4%, and Kick at 2.04 billion, up 30.7% , while YouTube's live hours fell 13.7% to 13.62 billion. A creator who broadcasts on two platforms and republishes on a third spreads one session's audience across three sets of numbers, and the creator economy has no common measure that adds them up.
 The game had been shaping ad markets before anyone could play it. On November 6, Ziff Davis chief executive Vivek Shah said the gaming ad market had been weak because of a light release slate ahead of the launch , and expected other publishers to market games they had held back, mostly in 2027. Roblox built modest headwinds from the release into its fourth-quarter guidance and noted that it is a console-only title, the same limitation Asmongold spent nine hours complaining about. Attention attracts fraud as well: in September, Surfshark projected that Grand Theft Auto 6-themed web domains would pass 750 by launch , up from 212 found by mid-August.
 For brand suitability , the transcript is a usable sample of what tentpole creator content sounds like. PPC Land counted 952 masked profanities over nine hours, about 105 an hour, along with crude sexual jokes, a disability slur used twice by the streamer about himself, and his repeated joke that the game was "written by women". None of that is unusual for live game streaming. It is, though, the context that a "gaming" or "GTA VI" targeting line buys around this launch, and the public view count no longer separates a person watching on a phone from an estimated sofa of people watching on a television.
 The comments are part of the same page. On this video, the comments shown first dealt with violence against protesters, "HR women" and the two leads, much of it repeating jokes the creator had made on stream, and the oldest of them held about 71% of the likes on the 18 that PPC Land quotes. None dealt with the brands, apps and media the game parodies. For an advertiser placed on or near the video, that is the conversation underneath the placement, separate from anything said in the nine hours above it. One comment, @d_j_c009's "So glad Asmongold is playing this so I don't have to", with about 5,300 likes, describes a viewer for whom the creator stands in for the purchase: a view for the channel, and an open question for the publisher.
 What the recording does not show
 The page does not display the video's running length, the date or platform of the original live broadcast, or whether the upload carries ads. The captions are automatic and contain errors: the bank's name appears as "Fleica" and "Fissa", "Colonel Sanders" as "Ker Sanders", errand boy as "Aaron boy", and Baldur's Gate as "Balders's Gate". Viewer claims about a PC release date, removed content and a protest scene were read aloud or repeated on the stream but not shown or confirmed. Only 20 of the 14,000 comments were displayed at 20:02 UTC, in YouTube's order; like counts above 1,000 are rounded; the claims about the game made in comments are unverified; and the page does not show whether any commenting account is automated.

 Summary
 Who: Asmongold, a streamer whose YouTube channel Asmongold TV has 4.76 million subscribers, and Rockstar Games, publisher of Grand Theft Auto VI. Viewers and commenters on the video, and advertisers buying gaming audiences around the launch.
 What: A recording of just over nine hours in which Asmongold, playing a Grand Theft Auto game for the first time, works through the opening of Grand Theft Auto VI on an Xbox, rates it "like a nine", predicts it will win game of the year and argues it should not because it is not on PC. The recording also documents the game's parodies of social media, fintech apps, ride-hailing, wellness resellers, AI and sponsored radio. The comment section, with 14,000 comments, was led by complaints about limits on violence, "HR women" and the two leads, many echoing the streamer's own jokes, and the 20 comments displayed at 20:02 UTC did not mention the parodies at all.
 When: The video was published today, November 19, 2026, the game's release day. By 20:02 UTC it showed 2,358,707 views.
 Where: On YouTube, on the Asmongold TV channel. The game is set in Leonida, Rockstar's fictional version of Florida, including the Keys and Vice City.
 Why: Grand Theft Auto VI is one of the largest entertainment launches of the year and has already shaped ad forecasts at Ziff Davis, Roblox and Microsoft. Long creator recordings like this one are where much of the launch audience gathers, and they come with public view counts that now include modelled TV co-viewers, heavy profanity and a heated argument in the comments, all of which advertisers buying around the game have to weigh.
